docs.title: A note on this edition
docs.text:
This is the text of The Institutes of Nārada, nāradīya Dharmaśāstra, translated by Julius Jolly (Trübner, 1876). It was made from the scan held by the Internet Archive (in.ernet.dli.2015.163377): the pages were read by machine and the text has not been proofread.

What is here. The text of the book, pages 5–168 of the scan, with the author's footnotes where the machine could tell them from the text. Left out: the title pages and the printed table of contents (the library makes its own), the index, whose references are to the pages of the printed book, advertisements and library stamps.

How it was made. Each page of the scan was cleaned and read with the Tesseract engine (version 5), using a model trained on proofread letterpress English with transliterated Sanskrit. Running heads and page numbers were taken out, the lines of each paragraph joined, words broken at the end of a line rejoined, and footnotes linked to their marks; the chapters follow the book's own.

How good it is. On scans like this the machine gets roughly one or two characters in a hundred wrong, more in footnotes, in Sanskrit words with diacritics, in tables, and at drop capitals at the start of a chapter or poem. Words printed in Devanagari or another non-Latin script are not read: they are shown as [Skt.] or as the machine's guess. Where the text matters, check it against the scan.

3 On Courts of Junstire. 4 1. One who is not appointed to le a member of the ba court must on no account speak at the trial of a law.

suit ; but by him, who has been appointed, an impartial bo opinion ought to bo given. 5 2. Whether appointed or not appointed, one who is 4 conversant with the law has a right to speak; for he ¹ ² whose conduct is regulated by the law, delivers a speech Śf inspired by the deity. â ¹ 3. For the trial of all law-suits persons familiar with 5 many branches of science should be appointed ; no Ś prudent man would entrust this task to a single person, ¹ ug though a virtuous one. ¹Ś 4. Whatever judgement ten men versed in the Veda; a and jurisprudence, or three men familiar with the ¹5 Veda, pass upon the case in hand is right, and a valid sentence. Ś 5. The king alone, being the suprome ruler, is en- :Ś titled to decide knotty law-cases; therefore a private x man should not pass a sentence alone; his opinion 4 Ś would leave room for doubt. . 6. A judge, pronouncing a fair sentence, incurs 4 : neither enmity nor sin ; but one who speaks differently ² incurs both. Ś ² 7. The king should appoint, as members of the court, : honest men of tried integrity, who are able to support the burden of the administration of justice like bulls a bearing a heavy load. 8. The assessors of the king's courts of judicature i should be men skilled in matters of law, sprung from good families, veracious, and impartial towards friend and foe. is ¹ 9. Divine justice is represented as a bull, and the i gods consider him who impedes justice as a Vyishala, i or one who slays a bull. Let no man therefore violate justice. ¹ 10. The only firm friend who follows you, even after hs death, is justice; everything else is extinct with the a body. 11. When law-suits are justly decided, the judges et obtain their own absolution. 37. A child is comparable to an embryo up to his eighth year; a boy is called pauganda (youth) up to & HH his sixteenth year. &

On Evidence by Writing. ² 1. Those conversant with the rules of evidence x by must pay a strict regard to the evidence; evidence ¹ loses its force, when it has not its due form. 2. Written proof, witnesses, and possession, these are the three kinds of evidence, on which the right of property rests, and by means of which a creditor may recover his loan. 5 3. A document remains always evidence, witnesses ; as long as they live, and possession becomes evidence Ś after a lapse of time ; thus it is propounded in the law-books. 4. What a man is not possessed of, that is not his123 own through the effect of possession, although the proprietor is known to be alive.

6. Whatever property a proprietor sees with his own - eyes being enjoyed by strangers, without for ten years asserting his rights, may not be recovered by him.

7. Because he has been indulgent and looking on without asserting his rights, therefore he will be non. D suited, if [cf. Cl. 3] he prefers a claim after the expiration ef the above-mentioned period.

8. If he is neither an idiot nor a mere child, and if the chattel is being enjoyed by a stranger while he is near, his property in it is extinct by law, and the adverse possessor shall keep it.

9. Pledges, boundaries, the property of children, common deposits, sealed deposits, women, and goods belonging to the king or learned Brahmins are not lost to the omer through their being possessed by a stranger.

10. Even pledges etc., are lost, if strangers have i enjoyed them for twenty years before the owner's eyes ; the property of women and of kings is excepted from this rule.

11. The property of women and of kings can never be lost, even though it be enjoyed for hundreds of years by strangers who have no title to it.

12. Where possession exists, but no title whatever exists, there a title, but not possession alone, can confer proprietary rights.

13. A title having been substantiated, the possession becomes valid ; 'it remains invalid without a proved title.

14. He who simply declares himself possessed of a commodity without having a title to it, is to be considered as a thief, in consequence of his pleading such illegitimate possession.

16. He who enjoys without a title for ever so many years, the king of the land should inflict on that e sinner the punishment of a thief. i ¹ 17. What a man possesses without a title, he must not alienate, being only the possessor of it ; but after the death of the possessor such possessions devolve upon his family. g 18. In cases falling within the memory of man possession of land with a title makes evidence. In ¹ cases extending beyond the memory of man, the u hereditary succession of three ancestors is admitted as be)

evidence, though the title be not produced.

19. I a man is accused by him whom he has injured by taking possession of his property, he can- ŚŚ : "not escape defeat; only what has formerly been Ś possessed by his fathers, and inherited by him in order, sy i is his legitimate property. ¹

20. When possession has been held, even mn.

lawfully, by three ancestors, including the father of (a the present occupant, that cannot be taken away from him, as having gone in order through three lives. ŚŚ ¹ 21. Common deposits, stolen goods, unspecified deposits, deposits for whose delivery a certain period . has been fixed (?), and what is being possessed in ¹ secret, are six things possessed without a title. i t 22. If a litigant dies while a law-suit about posses- 5 ( sions of his is pending, the son has to prove his. i title, the fact of his possession being insufficient to 5 i decide the suit. 4 . 23. What has been in the hands of three ancestors g Smârts Kâls, which is fixed at. 100 years by the Mitâksharâ. I See Appendix. 2 for a very long time, though they had no title, cannot be lost, having gone in order through three lives.

24. After the death of a creditor even witnesses are no longer of avail, except if a statement made by the creditor himself on his death-bed has been preserved. i

25. For after the death of an adversary the deposi- ™ tion of his witnesses loses its force, an attested 2 document only being capable of influencing the sentence in this case. = 26. But if a man not unsound in mind has preferred a legitimate claim, a witness may give evidence even after the claimant's death, in case it be in a matter touching the six cases of deposit and the rest.

27. In all business transactions the latest act shall;

; prevail, but in the case of a gift, a pledge, or a purchase, the prior act has the greater force. ¹ 28. A contract of delivery and receipt may be made with a view to gain by the lender on the principal sum while remaining with the debtor ; it is called a loan on interest, and money-lenders acquire their substance by it.

29. Interest on loans is of four kinds, according to the law-books : interest paid on an undiminished

principal (kâyikd), periodical interest (kâlikâ), stipu-45

lated interest (kâritâ), and compound interest (chakra- Ś eriddhâ). ul

30. Interest at the rate of one paṇa or half of a f paṇa, paid always, without diminishing the principal ee

(kâyâ) is termed kâyikâ ;t that which runs by the pr month, is named kâlikâ (from kâla " time expired.) 4

Contests regarding Boundaries. ¹

9. Let not one man alone fix the boundaries, how ever trustworthy he may be ; this duty ought to be performed by many, on account of its responsibility.

10. If a man were to fix them alone, let him do so.

That the Institutes of Nârada belong to a. later period than the bulk of any of the Dharmasttras—for some of them are full of subsequent additionscan be proved, even if we are prepared to admit that : the composition of prose works in the SŚtra style had not entirely ceased when the composition of metrical

3. A pupil, an apprentice, a hired servant, and, in ² the fourth place, an agent, are the free labourers ; slaves ¹ ¹ are those born in the house, and so forth. I

4. The learned have said that all these owe a certain degree of dependence ; but their respective rank and wages depend on their caste and the work A they do. od

5. There are two kinds of work to be distinguished ³ l —pure and impure work. What is done by the servant ²12 : 7. Attending the master at his pleasure, and rub- 7 bing him, are to be considered as impure work, and all ; other work as pure. : 8. A pupil shall obey his teacher till he has mastered ; science ; he shall equally obey his master's wife and son.

9. A pupil shall collect alms, and take his food

(pali) on a low seat, free from conceit. His couch ¹ shall be humble ; and he shall salute all those who kve i in his teacher's house first, when he meets them. 2 10. He shall never appear before his teacher, or I stay with him without his permission; and he shall { unflinchingly do the work he has been bid to do, if he can. ¹ 11. He shall read in the proper time, and if he has not been forbidden to do so by his master ; and sit at his master's feet or by his head in an attentive attitude.

12. His teacher shall reprimand him if he does not obey him ; for neglecting his reading, he shall be chastised with a rope or the small shoot of a cane.

13. The. teacher must not, in chastising and correcting him, beat him severely, nor on a noble part, nor on the breast ; by acting otherwise the teacher becomes liable to punishment from the king.

14. Having finished his course of study, let him offer his leaving-present to his teacher and return home. These are the rules of conduct for a pupil.

15. Let him who wishes to acquire his art, with the assent of his kinsmen, reside with an instructor, after

having fixed a certain period of apprenticeship.

16. The teacher shall instruct him, keep him in his own house, give him food, and not employ him in other work, but treat him as a son.

17. He who deserts a good instructor, who has given him the benefit of his teaching, shall be com- ¹ pelled by forcible means to stay with him, and is liable to whipping and confinement..

18. An apprentice must reside with his instructor till his time is out, even if he acquire his art before the ² expiration of it. As long as he is doing work there, his instructor shall take the profit of it.

19. Having acquired his art within the fixed time, the apprentice shall offer to the instructor the best reward in his power, and depart with his permission. Ś

20. There are three classes of labourers, the highest, ¹ : middle, and lowest class. The payment they get for g their labour is fixed according to their proficiency, and ¹ to the benefit derived from their exertions. I 221I. The highest class includes soldiers ; the middle ¹ class, servants employed in husbandry; the lowest 4 ¹ class, carriers of burdens : such is the threefold division of labourers. ¹ : 22. He to whom the management of business or the superintendence of the family is entrusted, is likewise to be reckoned among the free labourers; he is also 2 termed family-servant.

23. These are the four descriptions of labourers who do pure work ; all the rest do impure work, and are slaves, whereof there are fifteen kinds.

24. One born in the house, one bought, one re- Ś ceived by donation, one got by inheritance, one maintained in a famine, one pledged by a former Ś master, ) A

25. One relieved from a great debt, one made prisoner in a war, one obtained through a wager, one a who has offered himself, saying, I am thine," an apostate from religious mendicity, a slave for a fixed Ś period,

26. One maintained in reward of the work per- : formed by him, a slave for the sake of his wife, and : one self-sold, are the fifteen kinds of slaves declared by â the law. : 27. Of these, the first four cannot be released from slavery, unless they be emancipated by the generosity of their masters. Their servitude is hereditary.

28. However, if a slave saves the life of his master, when he is in peril, he is released from slavery, and obtains a son's share.

29. One maintained in a famine is released from slavery on giving a pair of oxen ; for what has been consumed in a famine is not discharged by labour alone.

30. One pledged is released when his master re-deems him by paying the debt; but if the creditor takes him in place of payment, he becomes a purchased slave.

31. A debtor is released from bondage by the payment of his debt with interest; a slave for a fixed period after the expiration of such period.

32. One who has offered himself, saying, “I am thine ; one made prisoner in a war ; and one obtained through a wager, recover their liberty on giving a substitute equally capable of labour.

33. An apostate from religious mendicity shall be the king's slave. He cannot be emancipated, for there is no atonement for his crime.

34. One maintained in consideration of work performed by him, is immediately released on relinquishing his subsistence ; and a slave for the sake of his wife is emancipated if he separates himself from her.
